dubious

/DOO-bee-uhs/ - the stress falls on DOO · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Dubious means doubtful, of uncertain quality.

Even nine-year-old Tess found the coupon's promise of a free island vacation dubious.

Example

The convertible gleamed, but its history was dubious: 40,000 miles on the dial, three owners in two years, and a service record that skipped 2019 entirely. Nothing proved the odometer lied; everything invited you to wonder.

Dubious captures a claim that invites doubt on its face: the mileage may be true, but three owners and a missing year make believing it feel unwise. Notice the word works two ways - the buyers were dubious (they felt the doubt), and the mileage was dubious (it caused the doubt).

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

questionable: Questionable is doubt at its mildest and most polite: the claim invites a second look, and the question is still open. Dubious has already leaned - the eyebrow is up, and believing feels unwise. A questionable receipt gets checked; a dubious one gets checked by someone frowning.

suspect: Suspect means already sitting under a cloud - suspicion has hardened into a working assumption that something is wrong, often dishonestly so. Dubious is a stage earlier and broader: quality or truth in real doubt, but no accusation yet. Results can be dubious through sloppiness; they turn suspect when someone may have cooked them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

trustworthy: safe to believe without checking twice

proven: already shown to be true or sound

Where it sits · how badly the claim strains belief

iffy → dubious → implausible

iffy vs. dubious: Iffy is a shrug - the picnic might still happen, but take an umbrella; dubious goes further, meaning the doubt has real teeth.

implausible vs. dubious: Implausible sits above dubious on the ladder: a dubious claim raises eyebrows, while an implausible one collides head-on with common sense.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — dubi: wavering between two

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together: Dubi (wavering between two) + -ous (full of) = full of two-mindedness. Latin dubium - built on duo, 'two' - named the state of being pulled toward two answers at once; a dubious claim leaves you hanging between believing and not.

Use the root in a new word: doubt: By the final lap her lead was indubitable, and even the rival coaches stopped checking their stopwatches.

Word Choice

neutral, mildly critical

Dubious carries a raised eyebrow: the claim, prize, or honor already smells off. Unverified, its no-judgment cousin in this unit, just means unchecked - say dubious only when doubt has actually set in. And it runs both directions: you can be dubious about a scheme, or the scheme itself can be dubious.
